source.title: Aquatic myofascial release applied after high intensity exercise increases flexibility and decreases pain

paper.citation: Costa Lêdo, V. R., Xavier, A. P., de Souza, C. A. Z., Fernandes, S. M. S., Rodrigues, É., & Caperuto, É. C. (2018). Aquatic myofascial release applied after high intensity exercise increases flexibility and decreases pain. Journal of Bodywork and Movement Therapies, 22(1), 97–104. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jbmt.2017.05.013
paper.abstract: Does 50 minutes of aquatic myofascial release after high-intensity resistance exercise alter flexibility and perceived soreness compared with 50 minutes without the intervention? Participants: 15 physically active men and women, mean age 25.7 ± 5.3 years. Setting: Laboratory resistance exercise followed by control and intervention phases separated by two weeks. Training or return-to-play context: Acute post-exercise recovery in healthy active adults, not injured athletes or in-season team-sport players. Inclusion and exclusion boundaries: Ages 18–28 and physically active; people with limiting muscle problems or fear/problems with pool immersion were excluded. Design: Within-participant two-phase comparison; randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding were not reported. Exposure or intervention: Six exercises, five sets of 15 repetitions at 80–90% estimated 1RM, followed by 50 minutes of aquatic myofascial release in warm water. Comparator: The same exercise protocol followed by 50 minutes without aquatic myofascial release, two weeks apart. Measurements and outcomes: Fingertip-to-floor and sit-and-reach flexibility, heart rate, blood lactate, Borg exertion, and visual-analogue pain ratings for seven days. Analysis: Normality testing and two-way ANOVA, with significance set at p < 0.05.
paper.tldr: This small within-participant study tests a combined warm-water and myofascial-release recovery session after a demanding resistance-exercise protocol, with immediate flexibility and seven-day soreness outcomes. Day-one pain was 4.47 ± 2.36 after the control phase and 1.13 ± 1.46 after the intervention; pain persisted through day six in control but reached zero by day five after intervention. Interpretation should remain within the reviewed population, design, and applicability limits.
paper.methods: Design: Within-participant two-phase comparison; randomization, allocation concealment, and blinding were not reported. Exposure or intervention: Six exercises, five sets of 15 repetitions at 80–90% estimated 1RM, followed by 50 minutes of aquatic myofascial release in warm water. Comparator: The same exercise protocol followed by 50 minutes without aquatic myofascial release, two weeks apart. Measurements and outcomes: Fingertip-to-floor and sit-and-reach flexibility, heart rate, blood lactate, Borg exertion, and visual-analogue pain ratings for seven days. Analysis: Normality testing and two-way ANOVA, with significance set at p < 0.05.
paper.findings: Day-one pain was 4.47 ± 2.36 after the control phase and 1.13 ± 1.46 after the intervention; pain persisted through day six in control but reached zero by day five after intervention. Sit-and-reach improved in the intervention phase from 24.79 ± 9.91 cm before exercise to 27.67 ± 9.46 cm after aquatic myofascial release. Fingertip-to-floor distance after the intervention was 11.03 ± 8.96 cm versus 12.80 ± 4.69 cm after the control recovery period, with lower distance representing greater reach. Post-exercise heart rate and lactate rose similarly in both phases and returned toward resting values by the final measurement.
paper.limitations: The sample was small and no a priori power calculation was performed, as the authors acknowledge. A combined intervention cannot separate effects of warm-water immersion, therapist contact, self-release, 50 minutes of rest, expectation, or the myofascial technique. Fixed phase order, randomization, assessor blinding, and participant blinding were not reported, leaving order and expectancy bias unresolved. Flexibility was tested about one hour after exercise, before typical delayed-onset soreness peaks; acute range changes do not establish faster performance recovery. Pain was self-reported, and the study did not measure muscle damage or inflammation biomarkers; claims about reduced inflammation exceed the measured outcomes. Healthy active adults performing a laboratory protocol are not a direct proxy for trained athletes, competition congestion, injury rehabilitation, or return to play.
paper.practicalImplications: The intervention may be considered an optional short-term comfort and range-of-motion strategy when pool access, staffing, and athlete preference justify 50 minutes. Do not infer tissue healing, restored readiness, or performance benefit from pain and flexibility alone; pair any trial with team-specific recovery, subsequent performance, and adverse-response measures.
paper.athleteDev: For athlete-development decisions, use this evidence only within the reviewed population and context. paper.rtp: For rehabilitation and return-to-sport decisions, the intervention may be considered an optional short-term comfort and range-of-motion strategy when pool access, staffing, and athlete preference justify 50 minutes. Do not infer tissue healing, restored readiness, or performance benefit from pain and flexibility alone; pair any trial with team-specific recovery, subsequent performance, and adverse-response measures. This study alone does not establish clearance criteria or a complete return-to-sport progression.
